brahmi.name: Brahmi
brahmi.summary: Every Thai letter traces back to this ancient Indian script, best known from the rock and pillar edicts of Emperor Ashoka.
facts: An abugida: each consonant carries an inherent /a/, and other vowels attach around it, the same principle Thai still uses.
Ashoka’s edicts, from the middle of the 3rd century BCE, are among its earliest securely dated examples.
Written left to right, unlike its northwestern contemporary Kharosthi.
brahmi.change: Gave Thai its core idea: consonant-first writing, with vowels as marks attached to the consonant.

pallava.name: Pallava
pallava.summary: A rounder southern form of Brahmi used by the Pallava dynasty. It sailed to Southeast Asia with traders, monks and Brahmins.
facts: Sanskrit and local-language inscriptions in Pallava letters turn up from South India to Cambodia and Java.
Each new home adapted it on its own, which is why Mon, Khmer, Cham and Javanese look related but distinct.
Letters became more rounded and ornamental than Brahmi’s angular forms.
pallava.change: Supplied the southern letter shapes that every Southeast Asian script, Thai included, still echoes.

old-khmer.name: Old Khmer
old-khmer.summary: The direct parent of Thai. The Angkor empire wrote with it, and its reach included much of today’s Thailand.
facts: Dated Old Khmer inscriptions begin in 611 CE and are found across Cambodia, southern Laos and Thailand.
Thai calls it อักษรขอม (akson khom) and still uses a Khom form for Pali and sacred texts.
Thai also borrowed many Khmer words, e.g. เดิน (to walk).
old-khmer.change: Provided the letter shapes and consonant inventory that Sukhothai would simplify.

sukhothai.name: Sukhothai script
sukhothai.summary: Tradition credits King Ram Khamhaeng with devising the Thai alphabet in 1283, adapting Old Khmer letters to the sounds of Tai speech.
facts: Its big invention was tone marks. Thai is often described as the first script to write tones with dedicated marks.
Letters were set in one straight line: no stacked consonants, and vowels at first sat on the same line too.
The Ram Khamhaeng Stele, found in 1833, is the key source, but scholars still debate how old it really is.
sukhothai.change: A fully Tai script: simpler letters, tone marks, and text that runs in a single line.

ayutthaya.name: Ayutthaya
ayutthaya.summary: In a large royal court on the Chao Phraya plain the script settles into the shapes we read today, with vowels moving above, below and before the consonant.
facts: By the late Ayutthaya period all four tone marks ◌่ ◌้ ◌๊ ◌๋ are in use.
Chindamani, attributed to Phra Horathibodi in the reign of King Narai (1656–1688), is generally regarded as the oldest Thai textbook.
Visitors from France under King Narai, such as Simon de la Loubère (1691), described the alphabet for European readers.
The fall of Ayutthaya to Burma in 1767 destroyed many manuscripts.
ayutthaya.change: Letter forms and spelling conventions settle, and vowels and tone marks reach their modern positions.

rattanakosin.name: Rattanakosin and print
rattanakosin.summary: Bangkok’s new dynasty brings printing presses and typewriters. Handwritten manuscripts give way to type, and spelling is standardized.
facts: Missionaries such as Dan Beach Bradley, in Bangkok from 1835, brought printing presses and published the Bangkok Recorder (1844).
In 1892 Edwin McFarland built the first Thai typewriter, which had to fit consonants, vowels and tone marks onto one keyboard.
Schools opened under King Mongkut (Rama IV) and King Chulalongkorn (Rama V) spread one standard spelling.
rattanakosin.change: Print fixes letter shapes and spelling, and handwriting stops being the main way Thai is copied.

modern.name: Modern Thai
modern.summary: A stable script with 44 consonant letters, four tone marks and dozens of vowel forms, now typed on every phone.
facts: A 1942 reform under Phibun tried to trim many letters and vowel signs, but it was largely undone after 1944.
ฃ and ฅ remain in the alphabet but are no longer used.
Computers encode Thai in the Unicode block U+0E00–U+0E7F.
The same script also writes Southern Thai, Isan and Northern Thai, as well as Pali.
modern.change: Familiar and stable: the script you are now learning to build, syllable by syllable.

devanagari.name: Devanagari
devanagari.note: Grew out of Gupta and Nagari forms. Writes Sanskrit, Hindi and Nepali, with a headline bar above the letters.

tamil.name: Tamil
tamil.note: Tamil-Brahmi evolved into the round modern Tamil script, which keeps only the consonants that Tamil needs.

old-mon.name: Old Mon
old-mon.note: Script of Dvaravati in central Thailand. It later gave rise to Burmese and to Tai Tham, and may have touched a few Sukhothai letters.

cham.name: Cham
cham.note: One of the oldest Brahmic scripts in Southeast Asia, used by the Champa kingdoms of central Vietnam.

javanese.name: Kawi and Javanese
javanese.note: Old Javanese Kawi script, ancestor of Javanese, Balinese and Sundanese writing.

khmer.name: Khmer
khmer.note: Modern Khmer keeps the stacked-consonant style that Thai gave up.

khom-thai.name: Khom Thai
khom-thai.note: The Khom letters as used in Thailand, mainly for Pali scriptures, amulets and yantra.

tai-tham.name: Tai Tham (Lanna)
tai-tham.note: Came from Old Mon and served Buddhist texts in the north. “Tham” means Dhamma.

fakkham.name: Fak Kham
fakkham.note: A northern variant of Sukhothai script used in Lanna. The name means “tamarind pod”, after its curved strokes.

tai-viet.name: Tai Dam (Black Tai)
tai-viet.note: Script of the Black Tai of northwest Vietnam. Some sources say it may be as old as, or older than, Sukhothai script.

lao.name: Lao
lao.note: Thai’s closest sister, reached through Fak Kham and Tai Noi. It drops extra Pali-Sanskrit consonants so spelling follows speech.
